title: Advisory: removing no more than about a third of a bush in one session (general pruning guidance, not rose-specific)

common.applies_to: Established Hybrid Tea, Floribunda or Grandiflora bush rose (a rose that has passed PKR-SGT-000003); dormant pruning
common.preserved_uncertainty: This is a general rule for shrubs and trees, not tested on roses. One rose-specific source recommends a hard, one-time renovation instead, which suggests the rule is a cautious default rather than a rose requirement (AF-40). The NC State wording is about a plant's crown in any one year, not about a single session (WEAKCONGESTED AF-18). No source links the choice between one hard cutback and a staged approach to a particular bush's condition (AF-40). A fifth source listed for AF-40 (Colorado State University, Adams County) couldn't be confirmed and isn't cited. Rose sources measure the amount removed in different ways (share of growth, of height, or of cane length), so their figures and the one-third rule may not measure the same thing (ARC-BUSHROSE-HARDPRUNE-01 C-3).

content.heading: How much to remove
content.label: General pruning guidance, with what rose growers do

items.text: One source says to remove no more than about a third of a plant's top growth in any one year.
If an overgrown bush needs a lot taken off, some sources spread the work over two or three years, about a third at a time.
Some rose sources renovate an old rose in one go instead of in stages.
At winter pruning rose growers commonly remove from a third to two-thirds of a Hybrid Tea's or Floribunda's growth or height, with half to two-thirds the most usual figure.
Rose sources disagree on what to call cutting back by a third: some call it "light" pruning, and another calls it "moderate".
